processing: Made as a green tea, typically spread, fixed by heat, rolled and dried.
harvest_season: Picked across the growing year, and spring, summer and autumn leaf smell measurably different. As with other Chinese greens, early spring buds are the usual prize.
appearance_dry: Tight, needle-like green strips with plenty of visible white down.
appearance_liquor: Clear, pale yellow-green, sometimes faintly cloudy from the down.
appearance_wet: Tender olive-green leaves with fuzzy undersides.
taste_profile: Rich and fresh with a chestnut note and a sweet finish, firmer and more bitter than a small-leaf green if steeped hard.

brewing.notes: Glass or a porcelain gaiwan, with cooler water than you would use for a small-leaf green, because this leaf turns bitter quickly. Pull it earlier if the first cup bites.

vintage_note: Sold as a current-year tea like other Chinese greens; drink it within a year. Lingyun leaf is also promoted for other tea classes, so check that the bag says green.
description:
Lingyun Baihao comes from Lingyun County in the Baise area of western Guangxi, mainly around the misty Cenwang Laoshan and Qinglong mountains. The name means white down, after the thick fuzz on the underside of the leaf, and the older name Lingyun Baimao says the same thing.

The plant matters as much as the place. The white-down leaf gives a strong cup that can turn bitter if handled roughly, so the brew matters.

Expect a full, fresh green with chestnut and a sweet finish. Lab work on its aroma found linalool and geraniol among the main compounds and clear differences by season: autumn leaning minty and floral, spring fruity, summer towards citrus. Use cooler water and short steeps; most bad cups here are simply overextracted.

It is sold as a regional name protected as a geographical indication, with the leaf also promoted as suitable for all six tea classes, a claim best read as marketing. Look for plenty of down, a named harvest and the words green, black or white on the pack.
history: The firm dates begin in the twentieth century. Lingyun tea was shown at the 1915 Panama exposition, where regional accounts credit it with a second prize. It was recorded in Chinese tea reference books in 1994 and took a Zhongcha Cup famous tea title in 1999.
